# Why Sulfur is Important in Lincosamide Antibiotics

**Authors:** Kelvin J. Y. Wu; Elena V. Aleksandrova; Paul J. Robinson; Amy E. Benedetto; Meiyi Yu; Ben I. C. Tresco; Dominic N. Y. See; Tong Jiang; Antonio Ramkissoon; Clémence F. Dunand; Maxim S. Svetlov; Joonho Lee; Yury S. Polikanov; Andrew G. Myers

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA. | 2Department of Biological Sciences, University of Illinois at Chicago, Chicago, IL 60607, USA. | 3Department of Pharmaceutical Sciences, University of Illinois at Chicago, Chicago, IL 60607, USA. | 4Center for Biomolecular Sciences, University of Illinois at Chicago, Chicago, IL 60607, USA. | 5These authors contributed equally. | 6Lead contact.

## Abstract

We recently reported the conception and synthesis of cresomycin (CRM), a fully synthetic lincosamide antibiotic effective in vitro and in vivo against multidrug-resistant Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. In this work, we describe the chemical synthesis and characterization of CRM sulfur atom replacement analogs C-CRM (S → CH2), O-CRM (S → O), and Se-CRM (S → Se). Comparison of high-resolution co-crystal structures showed that the four analogs adopted identical conformations when bound to the bacterial ribosome, but due to variations of ≤1 Å in the bond lengths between the anomeric carbon and the varied atoms, only the S and Se heteroatoms of CRM and Se-CRM, respectively, were positioned to interact with the π-face of nucleobase G2505. C-CRM and O-CRM did not benefit from such stabilizations, with correspondingly negative consequences in both target engagement and antibacterial activities. We therefore conclude that the sulfur atom of the lincosamides is important in ribosomal binding.

## Abstract

We describe the chemical syntheses, MIC analyses, biochemical profiling, ribosome-bound X-ray crystal structures, and computational studies of cresomycin (CRM) sulfur atom replacement analogs C-CRM (S → CH2), O-CRM (S → O), and Se-CRM (S → Se), making side-by-side comparisons with CRM. We show that the anomeric sulfur atom within lincosamide antibiotics participates in an essential S-π interaction with rRNA nucleobase G2505, and conclude that the sulfur atom is important for maintaining effective binding of the antibiotic to the bacterial ribosome.

## Abstract

## Introduction

The bacterial ribosome translates bacterial nucleic acid information molecules (RNA) into protein readout and is the primary target for multiple evolutionarily independent, structurally distinct classes of natural products with antibiotic activity.1,2 The lincosamides form one such class of antibiotics and inhibit protein synthesis by binding to the peptidyl transferase center (PTC) within the large (50S) ribosomal subunit.3 However, both of the two FDA-approved lincosamide antibiotics, lincomycin4 (1964) and clindamycin5 (CLI, 1970, Fig. 1a), are rapidly cleared in animals and humans by hepatic sulfoxidation.6,7 Recognizing the anomeric thioether group as a metabolic liability, researchers at Vicuron Pharmaceuticals8 and, subsequently, our own laboratory,9 employed chemical synthesis to prepare lincosamide sulfur atom replacement analogs, but invariably these analogs proved to be inferior antibiotic candidates in minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) analyses, with no clear explanation as to why. With the recent discovery of the fully synthetic macrobicyclic oxepanoprolinamide antibiotic cresomycin (CRM, Fig. 1a), which exhibits potent activity in both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial strains, including those expressing one or more genes conferring antimicrobial resistance (AMR) to CLI and other antibiotics, we saw an opportunity to investigate in a new context atomic replacement of the anomeric sulfur atom of CRM, which like CLI undergoes hepatic sulfoxidation, albeit at a significantly slower rate.10 In this work we describe the chemical syntheses, MIC analyses, biochemical profiling, ribosome-bound X-ray crystal structures, and computational studies of CRM sulfur atom replacement analogs C-CRM (S → CH2), O-CRM (S → O), and Se-CRM (S → Se), making side-by-side comparisons with CRM. The high-resolution crystal structures alongside antibacterial susceptibility measurements and computational analyses reveal why sulfur is important in targeting the bacterial ribosome.

## Results & Discussion

### Synthesis of CRM sulfur atom replacement analogs

The three CRM sulfur atom replacement analogs C-CRM, O-CRM, and Se-CRM were synthesized by routes that paralleled the discovery synthetic route to CRM, each featuring a tactical two-step sequence of low-temperature (−108 °C) crotylation of Ellman sulfinimine intermediates followed by a (Z)-selective ring-closing metathesis reaction using the Grubbs II catalyst.10 The C-, O-, and Se-glycosidic precursors C-1, O-1, and Se-1, respectively, were prepared in three steps each from known α-D-galactose derived precursors, as depicted in Fig. 1b. Thus, per-O-benzoylated α-D-galactopyranose11 underwent α-selective C-allylation upon exposure to allyltrimethylsilane and boron trifluoride etherate12; the product was then treated with 9-borabicyclo[3.3.1]nonane (9-BBN) and the resultant trialkylborane intermediate was subjected to B-alkyl Suzuki coupling with bromoethylene to furnish C-1 in 21% yield for the three-step sequence. Per-O-trimethylsilylated α-D-galactopyranose13 underwent α-selective O-glycoside formation with trimethylsilyl iodide and 3-buten-1-ol in the presence of tetrabutylammonium iodide14 (TBAI); the product was then subjected to global silyl deprotection and benzoyl reprotection to furnish O-1 in 57% yield for the three-step sequence. Per-O-acetylated p-toluoyl α-D-selenogalactopyranoside15 underwent Se-alkylation with 4-bromo-1-butene in the presence of piperazine and cesium carbonate15; the product was then subjected to global acetate deprotection and benzoyl reprotection to furnish Se-1 in 70% yield for the three-step sequence.

Intermediates C-1, O-1, and Se-1 were transformed via identical reaction sequences to afford C-CRM, O-CRM, and Se-CRM, respectively; as a representative example, the full synthetic sequence for the specific instance of C-CRM is illustrated in Fig. 2a. In brief, selective deprotection of the primary benzoyl group within C-1, followed by oxidation of the resulting primary alcohol with the Dess-Martin periodinane and condensation of the resultant aldehyde with (R)-tert-butylsulfinamide afforded the Ellman sulfinimine C-2 in 38% yield over three steps. Zinc-mediated crotylation of C-2 and subsequent Grubbs ring-closing metathesis afforded the (Z)-macrobicycle C-3 in 44% yield over two steps. Global benzoyl and sulfinamide deprotection gave the macrobicyclic amine C-4 in 36% yield over the two steps. Lastly, amide coupling of C-4 with the oxepanoproline southern fragment (1)16 followed by N-Boc deprotection afforded C-CRM in 44% yield over the two steps. The sulfur atom replacement analogs O-CRM (Fig. 2b) and Se-CRM (Fig. 2c) were prepared in analogous fashion; all three analogs were prepared in amounts sufficient for antimicrobial and biochemical profiling (>5 mg). Their 1H NMR spectra were remarkably similar to those of CRM (see supplementary information), which suggested that the conformations of the atomic replacement analogs were similar to CRM, a proposal that was borne out in X-ray crystallographic studies (vide infra).

### Antimicrobial and biochemical profiling of CRM, C-CRM, O-CRM, and Se-CRM

CRM, C-CRM, O-CRM, and Se-CRM were evaluated in broth microdilution antimicrobial analyses using a panel of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria (Fig. 3). The single-atom substitution of sulfur in CRM for CH2 (C-CRM) or oxygen (O-CRM) led to precipitous declines in antibacterial activity against all bacterial strains assessed. In contrast, the single-atom substitution of sulfur in CRM for selenium (Se-CRM) produced virtually no change in antibacterial activity against the same panel of isolates. When assessed in a human liver microsomal stability assay (Fig. 3, Supplementary Fig. 1, Supplementary Table 1), the half-life of O-CRM (119.9 min) was more than double the half-life of CRM (55.6 min) and more than quadruple the half-life of Se-CRM (27.2 min), highlighting a trend of decreased metabolic stability upon descension of the periodic table (from O to S to Se). The half-life of C-CRM in the presence of human liver microsomes (61.8 min) was only slightly longer than that of CRM (55.6 min). Interestingly, the only sulfur atom replacement analog that exhibited a marked improvement in metabolic stability (O-CRM) also showed the steepest decline in observed antibacterial activity.

To confirm that all four antibiotics (CRM, C-CRM, O-CRM, and Se-CRM) functioned by inhibiting the initiation of bacterial translation, we conducted primer extension inhibition (“toeprinting”) analysis17 upon all four molecules, the results of which strongly supported that conjecture (Supplementary Fig. 2). The antibacterial activity of an antibiotic targeting the bacterial ribosome can be viewed as a function of its membrane permeability, susceptibility to efflux, and target engagement.18 To elucidate the mechanistic underpinnings behind the improved antibacterial activities of CRM and Se-CRM compared to C-CRM and O-CRM, we first evaluated the effect of efflux on Gram-negative antibacterial activity using the efflux ratio, determined by dividing each antibiotic’s MIC against the wild-type E. coli strain (MP-4) by its MIC against an isogenic E. coli strain (MP-9) with loss-of-function mutations in the major efflux transporter gene tolC. CRM, C-CRM, O-CRM, and Se-CRM displayed similar efflux ratios ranging from 8 to 16 (Fig. 3), suggesting that the driver of antibacterial activity for CRM was not efflux avoidance. Next, we evaluated the effect of outer membrane permeability on Gram-negative antibacterial activity using the permeability ratio, determined by dividing each antibiotic’s MIC against the ΔtolC E. coli strain (MP-9) by its MIC against a hyperpermeable E. coli strain (MP-74) with a loss-of-function mutation in the outer-membrane assembly gene lptD. CRM, C-CRM, O-CRM, and Se-CRM displayed similar permeability ratios ranging from 0.25 to 0.5 (Fig. 3), suggesting that the driver of antibacterial activity for CRM was not membrane permeability. Lastly, the impact of target engagement was assessed, albeit indirectly, by measuring the concentrations necessary for each molecule to displace 50% of bound [14C]-radiolabeled erythromycin from purified E. coli 70S ribosomes (IC50) following literature precedent,19 with results rank-ordered from lowest to highest required concentrations as follows (Fig. 3, Supplementary Fig. 3): CRM (8.5 nM, the lower limit of detection of the assay), Se-CRM (18 nM), C-CRM (40 nM), and O-CRM (175 nM). These findings correlate qualitatively with the measured MIC values of the antibiotics in both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial strains, suggesting that the primary driver of antimicrobial activity in this series is target engagement.

### Structural basis for differential target engagement by CRM sulfur atom replacement analogs

To gain further insights into the details of target engagements, we determined X-ray crystal structures of C-CRM, O-CRM, and Se-CRM in complex with Thermus thermophilus (Tth) 70S ribosomes at 2.50-Å, 2.50-Å, and 2.45-Å resolution, respectively (Fig. 4, Supplementary Fig. 4, Supplementary Table 2). As in the reported crystal structure of CRM bound to the Tth 70S ribosome,10 all three crystal structures of the sulfur atom replacement analogs comprised identically-bound mRNA, deacylated tRNAPhe in the A and E sites, and aminoacylated fMet-tRNAiMet in the P site (Fig. 4a). The Fourier difference maps that were obtained for C-CRM, O-CRM, and Se-CRM crystal structures revealed strong positive electron density, allowing us to determine unambiguously each of their structures (Supplementary Fig. 4). The binding sites of C-CRM, O-CRM, and Se-CRM are nearly indistinguishable from that of CRM and reside at the peptidyl transferase center (PTC) of the Tth 70S ribosome (Supplementary Fig. 5a). In the southern hemisphere of all four antibiotics, the C4′-isobutyl group firmly engages the PTC by extending deep into the A-site cleft, occupying a hydrophobic pocket formed by the nucleobases A2451, C2452, and U2506 of the 23S rRNA (Supplementary Fig. 5b). This pocket normally accommodates the α-side chains of incoming aminoacyl tRNAs and plays a key role in positioning the aminoacylated 3′-end of A-site tRNA within the PTC during transpeptidation.20,21 In the northern hemisphere, the macrobicyclic fragment of each atomic replacement analog is anchored identically in the PTC by an extensive network of hydrogen bonds with nucleotides A2058, A2059, and A2503 of the 23S rRNA (Supplementary Fig. 5c, d).

An overlay of the structures of CRM, C-CRM, O-CRM, and Se-CRM showed that the four macrobicyclic rings were essentially identical conformationally, but revealed subtle differences in the positions of the S, C, O, and Se atoms, respectively, relative to the π-face of nucleobase G2505 (Fig. 4). The positions of these atoms are largely determined by the different lengths of their bonds to the anomeric carbon (C1, Fig. 4b). For example, for O-CRM, the C1–O bond length was 1.44 Å and the oxygen atom was 3.90 Å away from the closest atom (C4) of G2505. For C-CRM, the C1–C bond length was 1.56 Å and the carbon atom was 3.76 Å from C4 of G2505. For CRM, the C1–S bond length was 1.81 Å and the sulfur atom was 3.43 Å from C4 of G2505. For Se-CRM, the C1–Se bond length was 2.00 Å and the selenium atom was 3.34 Å from C4 of G2505. These observations support the hypothesis that CRM ribosomal binding benefits from an S–π interaction with nucleobase G2505, and explain the different ribosomal binding affinities of each atomic replacement analog. Thus, the sulfur and selenium atoms of CRM and Se-CRM, respectively, are sufficiently diffuse and well-positioned (by virtue of their longer C1–S and C1–Se bond lengths) to engage with the π-face of G2505. In contrast, the more compact Van der Waals (VDW) atomic radius and the shorter C1–O bond length of O-CRM place the oxygen atom too far away from G2505 to engage in an O–π interaction. Lastly, unlike the chalcogen-containing analogs, the anomeric methylene group of C-CRM has no lone-pair electrons to interact with G2505.

### Theoretical support for an S–π interaction in CRM ribosomal binding

To better understand the role of the sulfur atom of CRM relative to its atomic replacement analogs in ribosomal binding, we applied density functional theory (DFT) to assess the interaction energies of CRM and each sulfur atom replacement analog with the nucleobase G2505 using the minimal fragment model depicted in Fig. 5a.22 The DFT analyses were performed using the reported continuum dielectric constant of DNA (ε = 8.0023) to approximate the rRNA microenvironment and were validated using the Auxiliary-Field Quantum Monte Carlo24,25 (AFQMC) method (Supplementary Fig. 6). The DFT calculations (Fig. 5b) showed that O-CRM had the weakest interaction energy with G2505 (–4.88 kcal/mol), followed by C-CRM (–5.68 kcal/mol), CRM (–6.08 kcal/mol), then Se-CRM (–6.27 kcal/mol). Energy decomposition analysis was performed using the absolutely-localized molecular orbitals (ALMO-EDA) technique,26 which revealed that dispersion forces provided the primary attractive interaction for CRM and each sulfur atom replacement analog, and were weakest for O-CRM (–8.67 kcal/mol), followed by C-CRM (–8.86 kcal/mol), CRM (–10.40 kcal/mol), then Se-CRM (–11.54 kcal/mol), in accord with the structural and microbiological data presented above.

## Conclusion

The structurally distinct lincosamide natural products lincomycin and celesticetin27 (Supplementary Fig. 7), produced by different strains of Streptomyces using evolutionarily distinct biosynthetic pathways, are notably variant in both the northern and southern hemispheres, yet both retain a common anomeric sulfur atom as part of different thioether linkages. All semisynthetic lincosamide antibiotics approved for human (CLI, Fig. 1a) or veterinary (pirlimycin28, Supplementary Fig. 7) medicine similarly retain an anomeric thioether substituent, in spite of efforts to replace this group, as discussed above. The high-resolution ribosomal crystal structures reported herein, supported by state-of-the-art calculational studies, make evident the importance of VDW stabilization between the sulfur atom of CRM and the π-face of nucleobase G2505.3 The selenium atom of Se-CRM benefits from a similar stabilization upon ribosomal binding and displays MIC values in antibacterial screening that are nearly indistinguishable from those of CRM, but Se-CRM also displayed the shortest half-life (27.2 min) in the presence of human liver microsomes, which was perhaps to be expected. Apart from a remarkable atomic-level analysis of ribosomal binding by a series of PTC-targeting antibiotics, a daunting conclusion from inspection of the MIC table of Fig. 3 is the extraordinary sensitivity of antibacterial activities to structural perturbations arising from atomic variations that produce changes in bond lengths of less than an angstrom. Though we now view the sulfur atom of lincosamide antibiotics as essential, the anomeric thioether remains a metabolic liability in vivo; we have therefore employed strategies other than atomic replacement to attenuate hepatic oxidation. These include steric occlusion of the sulfur atom, as in CRM, and judicious placement of electron-withdrawing fluorine atoms near the sulfur atom, as in the antibiotic candidate BT-33.29

## METHODS

### Antibacterial susceptibility testing

In vitro antibiotic susceptibility testing was performed using the broth microdilution method in accordance with the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines.30 The chemical syntheses of C-CRM, O-CRM, and Se-CRM, alongside their associated NMR spectra, are outlined in the supplemental information. CRM was synthesized according to literature precedent.10 All test compounds were stored as dry powders at –20 ºC prior to use. Working solutions of test compounds were made at a concentration of 3.2 mg·mL–1 in DMSO immediately before use. Final antibiotic concentrations ranged from 32 – 0.06 μg∙mL–1, in steps of two-fold dilutions, and maintained a final DMSO concentration of 2%.

Bacterial isolates were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC; Manassas, VA, USA), JMI Laboratories Inc. (North Liberty, IA, USA), Micromyx repository (MMX; Kalamazoo, MI, USA), or Massachusetts Eye and Ear (Boston, MA, USA). All isolates were cryopreserved at –80 ºC in glycerol stocks (20% glycerol in species-specific media). All isolates were revived from cryopreservation and sub-cultured on brain heart infusion agar (BD Diagnostics; Sparks, MD, USA) at 37 ºC in 5% CO2 for 24 hours prior to experimentation.

For all organisms, 3–5 uniform colonies were picked from subcultures and suspended in 10 mL of cation-adjusted Mueller Hinton broth (ca-MHB) and incubated for 2–3 hours at 37 ºC while being shaken at 250 rpm. The bacterial suspensions were then adjusted to a 0.5 MacFarland standard and further diluted 1:200 in ca-MHB to obtain a final test inoculum of 5 × 105 CFU mL–1. 96-well plates were seeded with DMSO solutions of the test compounds in a two-fold serial dilution series. The final test inoculum of each organism in ca-MHB was then added and the plates were incubated for 18–24 hours at 37 ºC. MIC values were represented as the modal value of biological triplicate experiments.

### Hepatic microsomal stability

Hepatic microsomal stability was evaluated by incubating 1 μM of CRM, C-CRM, O-CRM, or Se-CRM with 1 mg/mL human hepatic microsomes in 100 mM potassium phosphate buffer at pH 7.4. The reaction was initiated by adding NADPH to achieve a final concentration of 1 mM. Aliquots were removed at 0, 5, 10, 20, 40, and 60 minutes and added to acetonitrile (5 × v:v, contains 10 ng/mL propranolol as internal standard) to stop the reaction and precipitate the protein. NADPH dependence of the reaction was evaluated with –NADPH samples. At the end of the assay, the samples were centrifuged through a Millipore Multiscreen Solvinert 0.45 μm low binding PTFE hydrophilic filter plate and analyzed by LC-MS/MS. Data was log-transformed and represented as half-lives.

### Competitive ribosomal binding assay with [14C]-erythromycin

A stock solution of E. coli ribosomes (20 nM, purified from MRE600 following literature precedent31 and stored in a buffer solution containing 20 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 7.6), 6 mM Mg(OAc)2, 50 mM NH4OAc, and 4 mM β-mercaptoethanol) and [14C]-erythromycin (20 nM, American Radiolabeled Chemicals Inc.) was prepared in binding buffer (1.5 mL per reaction, 20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.6), 10 mM MgCl2, 150 mM NH4Cl, and 6 mM β-mercaptoethanol) and incubated at 37 ºC for 30 minutes. 1.5 mL aliquots of this stock solution were dispensed into Eppendorf tubes, and CRM, C-CRM, O-CRM, or Se-CRM were added separately as solutions in DMSO (3 nM to 3000 nM, 0.1% DMSO final concentration). The reactions were incubated for 1 hour at 37 ºC. 20 μL of a manufacturer-supplied suspension (~50 mg/mL) of DEAE magnetic beads (Bioclone #FM101), pre-washed with H2O (1 × 1 mL) and binding buffer (2 × 1 mL), was added to each reaction. The resultant suspensions were incubated for an additional 15 minutes at 23 ºC. For each reaction, the beads were captured on a magnetic stand (Invitrogen), the supernatant was removed, and the beads were washed with ice-cold binding buffer (1 × 1 mL). 10 mM EDTA solution (100 μL) was added to the beads and the resultant suspension was incubated for 10 minutes at 23 ºC to release bound [14C]-erythromycin from the 70S ribosomes. The beads were re-captured on a magnetic stand and the eluent was transferred to scintillation vials containing 5 mL of liquid scintillation cocktail (PerkinElmer Ultima Gold). The radioactivity of each eluent solution was quantified by scintillation counting and the concentration of CRM, C-CRM, O-CRM, or Se-CRM at which half the bound radiolabeled erythromycin was displaced (IC50) was determined using Graphpad Prism 10.0.2 software.

### Primer extension inhibition (toeprinting) analysis

The primer extension inhibition (toeprinting) analysis of drug-dependent ribosome stalling was carried out using synthetic ermDL DNA template as previously described32 with minor modifications. In brief, toeprinting reactions were carried out in 5-μL aliquots containing PURExpress transcription-translation coupled system (New England Biolabs, USA), to which the DNA template was added. The reactions were incubated at 37 °C for 20–25 minutes. Reverse transcription on the templates was carried out using radioactively labeled primer NV1 (5′-GGTTATAATGAATTTTGCTTATTAAC-3′). Primer extension products were resolved on 6% denaturing sequencing gels. The final concentration of ERY, RET, CRM, O-CRM, C-CRM, or Se-CRM was 50 μM. In all reactions, we used 50 μM mupirocin (inhibitor of isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase) to arrest ribosomes at the Ile codon downstream of the macrolide arrest site (Supplementary Fig. 2).

### X-ray crystallographic structure determination

Wild-type 70S ribosomes from T. thermophilus (strain HB8) were prepared as described previously.20,21,33 Synthetic mRNA with the sequence 5′-GGC-AAG-GAG-GUA-AAA-AUG-UUC-UAA-3′ containing the Shine-Dalgarno sequence followed by the P-site methionine (AUG) and A-site phenylalanine (UUC) codons was obtained from Integrated DNA Technologies (Coralville, IA, USA). Ribosome complexes with mRNA and tRNAs were formed by incubating 5 μM T. thermophilus 70S ribosomes with 10 μM mRNA at 55°C for 10 minutes, followed by the addition of 20 μM fMet-tRNAiMet and 20 μM deacylated tRNAPhe substrates.10,21,34 For the ribosome complexes containing O-CRM, C-CRM, or Se-CRM, each compound was added to a final concentration of 100 μM, and the complexes were left at room temperature for an additional 15 minutes prior to crystallization. Ribosome complexes were prepared in the buffer containing 5 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 7.6), 50 mM KCl, 10 mM NH4Cl, and 10 mM Mg(OAc)2, and then crystallized in the buffer containing 100 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.6), 2.9% (w/v) PEG-20K, 9–10% (v/v) MPD, 175 mM arginine, 0.5 mM β-mercaptoethanol. Crystals were grown by the vapor diffusion method in sitting drops at 19 °C, then stabilized and cryo-protected stepwise using a series of buffers with increasing MPD concentrations (25%, 30%, 35%) until reaching the final concentration of 40% (v/v) MPD as described previously.10,21,34 The final 40% MPD stabilization buffer contained 100 μM of the corresponding compound. After stabilization, crystals were flash-frozen using a nitrogen cryo-stream at 80 K (Oxford Cryosystems, UK).

Collection and processing of the X-ray diffraction data, model building, and structure refinement were performed as previously described.10,20,21,33,34 Diffraction data were collected at beamlines 24ID-C and 24ID-E at the Advanced Photon Source (Argonne National Laboratory). A complete dataset was collected using 0.979Å X-ray irradiation at 100K from multiple regions of the same crystal, using 0.3-degree oscillations. Raw data were integrated and scaled using the XDS software package (version from Jan 10, 2022).35 Molecular replacement was performed using PHASER from the CCP4 program suite (version 7.0).36 The search model was generated from the previously published structures of the T. thermophilus 70S ribosome with bound mRNA and aminoacylated tRNAs (PDB entry 6XHW).37 Initial molecular replacement solutions were refined by rigid-body refinement with the ribosome split into multiple domains, followed by positional and individual B-factor refinement using the PHENIX software (version 1.17).38 Non-crystallographic symmetry restraints were applied to four parts of the 30S ribosomal subunit (head, body, spur, and helix 44) and four parts of the 50S subunit (body, L1-stalk, L10-stalk, and C-terminus of the L9 protein). Initial PDB models and CIF restraints for O-CRM, C-CRM, or Se-CRM were generated using the PRODRG online software.39 The final PDB model was built in Coot (version 0.8.2).40 The statistics of data collection and refinement are compiled in Supplementary Table 2. All figures showing atomic models were rendered using PyMOL Molecular Graphics System software (version 1.8.6, Schrödinger, www.pymol.org).

### Computational methods

All EDA + DFT, and RI-MP2 calculations were run with Q-Chem 6.0.26 The structures and locations of the ligand and binding pocket residues were extracted from the crystal structures via PyMOL.41 Because our simulations only aim to describe the differences in interactions between CRM, C-CRM, O-CRM, and Se-CRM, we truncate the analogs by replacing their amide groups with hydrogen atoms. We truncate the G2505 residue by replacing the ribose sugar with a methyl group.

The truncated residues and CRM analogs were independently geometry-optimized at the ωB97X-V/def2-TZVPD level of theory and then repositioned to maximally align with the original structure using PyMol. For the interacting complex, only the positions of the hydrogen atoms were optimized, also at the ωB97X-V/def2-TZVPD level of theory. The orientations of the hydroxyl groups on the CRM analogs were selected based on geometry optimizations of a larger system containing the additional nearby nucleobase A2058 at the ωB97X-V/def2-SVPD level of theory. This demonstrated that the hydroxyl groups participate in intermolecular hydrogen bonds rather than intramolecular ones.

We evaluated the exchange-correlation potential and non-local correlation with the SG-2 and SG-1 quadrature grids respectively.42,43 Following the literature,44 we checked for grid dependence with the very dense (99, 590) and (50,194) grids for the exchange correlation potential and non-local correlation, respectively. In the worst case (Se-CRM), the magnitude of the error introduced by a smaller grid is only 0.02, 0.07, 0.005, and 0.06 kcal/mol, respectively, for the interaction, frozen, polarization, and charge transfer energies. This provides confidence that the smaller grid is accurate.

While the DFT calculations conform with current best practices,44,45 we additionally compared against RI-MP2, a computationally efficient ab initio approach,46–48 and AFQMC, a quantum Monte Carlo method which has been demonstrated to provide gold-standard level accuracy in many classes of chemical systems while scaling to larger systems than CCSD(T) (Supplementary Fig. 6a).49–52 The calculations performed here provide a potential template for future drug discovery applications for molecules with stronger electronic correlation.53,54

The DFT results are in excellent agreement with the AFQMC results while MP2 overshoots the interaction energy, which is expected.55,56 AFQMC distinguishes O-CRM and Se-CRM as the weakest and strongest interactions, respectively, but does not resolve the ordering between CRM and C-CRM. These results do confirm, however, that DFT is an appropriate choice of methodology for further analysis.

EDA and PCM calculations were carried out following literature precedent44 and at the ωB97X-V/def2-TZVPD level of theory. All interaction energies are corrected for basis set superposition error via a counterpoise correction. The solvent accessible surface for PCM was generated with a 1.4 Å solvent probe radius and the results were BSSE corrected by using the BSSE correction from the gas phase calculation. We considered the effect of solvents with varying dielectric constants (Supplementary Fig. 6b); increasing the continuum dielectric constant lowers the interaction energy for CRM, O-CRM, and Se-CRM, while the interaction energy for C-CRM remains nearly constant. This suggests that in the full rRNA environment, C-CRM will have a weaker binding affinity than CRM, consistent with the experiments; however, direct calculations of binding free energies differences would be required for a more quantitative statement.57,58

The RI-MP2 calculations were performed on each system using the cc-pVTZ and cc-pVQZ basis sets and corresponding auxiliary basis sets.59–61 The CBS result was extracted via a two-point extrapolation of the RI-MP2 correlation energy from the following formula: ( E RI − MP 2 ) CBS = ( E HF ) QZ ∓ ( ( E c o r r RI − MP 2 ) QZ 4 3 − ( E c o r r RI − MP 2 ) TZ 3 3 ) 4 3 − 3 3 .

The AFQMC calculations were performed with ipie52,62 using RHF trials generated by PySCF.63 The Cholesky decomposition of the two electron integrals was found to introduce a minimal amount of error with a cutoff of 10−4 for C-CRM and O-CRM and 10−5 for CRM and Se-CRM. Because AFQMC calculations are computationally demanding, we approximate the CBS correction for AFQMC at the cc-pVTZ level with the RI-MP2 CBS extrapolation energy using the following formula: ( E AFQMC ) CBS = ( E AFQMC ) TZ ∓ ( ( E RI − MP 2 ) CBS − ( E RI − MP 2 ) TZ ) .

# Discovery of a fluorinated macrobicyclic antibiotic through chemical synthesis

**Authors:** Ben I. C. Tresco; Kelvin J. Y. Wu; Antonio Ramkissoon; Elena V. Aleksandrova; Michael Purdy; Dominic N. Y. See; Richard Y. Liu; Yury S. Polikanov; Andrew G. Myers

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA. | 2Department of Biological Sciences, University of Illinois at Chicago, Chicago, IL 60607, USA. | 3Department of Pharmaceutical Sciences, University of Illinois at Chicago, Chicago, IL 60607, USA. | 4Center for Biomolecular Sciences, University of Illinois at Chicago, Chicago, IL 60607, USA.

## Abstract

The emergence of bacterial antimicrobial resistance threatens to undermine the utility of antibiotic therapy in medicine. This threat can be addressed, in part, by reinventing existing antibiotic classes using chemical synthesis. Here we present the discovery of BT-33, a fluorinated macrobicyclic oxepanoprolinamide antibiotic with broad-spectrum activity against multidrug-resistant bacterial pathogens. Structure-activity relationships within the macrobicyclic substructure reveal structural features that are essential to the enhanced potency of BT-33 as well as its increased metabolic stability relative to its predecessors clindamycin, iboxamycin, and cresomycin. Using X-ray crystallography, we determine the structure of BT-33 in complex with the bacterial ribosome revealing that its fluorine atom makes an additional Van der Waals contact with nucleobase G2505. Through variable-temperature 1H-NMR experiments, density-functional theory calculations, and vibrational circular dichroism spectroscopy, we compare macrobicyclic homologs of BT-33 and a C7-desmethyl analog and find that the C7-methyl group of BT-33 rigidifies the macrocyclic ring in a conformation that is highly preorganized for ribosomal binding.

## Abstract

## Introduction

The natural product lincomycin (Fig. 1a), discovered by Upjohn scientists in 1962, was the first and defining member of the lincosamide class of antibiotics, and received approval by the FDA for use in humans in 19641. Subsequently, lincomycin was used as a starting material for the discovery of next generation lincosamide antibiotics. Clindamycin (CLI, Fig. 1a), the product of a single-step deoxy-chlorination reaction, was found to have improved pharmacokinetic properties relative to lincomycin, and in 1970 became the second of, to date, only two FDA-approved lincosamides2. The ensuing decades of use of (primarily) clindamycin in hospitals and the community have led to the acquisition and widespread dissemination of manifold mechanisms of resistance to lincosamides (and other antibiotics) in bacteria. These resistance mechanisms include two distinct rRNA methyltransferases (encoded by erm and cfr genes)3,4; ATP-binding cassette type F proteins (encoded by vgaA, lsaA, and cplR genes), which expel lincosamides from stalled ribosomes5,6; and lincosamide nucleotidyltransferases (encoded by lnu genes)7,8. Together, these genes confer resistance to >7 structurally distinct classes of ribosome-targeting antibiotics, including lincosamides, macrolides, oxazolidinones, streptogramins, and pleuromutilins. Although there has been no new lincosamide antibiotic to advance to human clinical trials since 1970, this has not been due to a lack of research effort. Using primarily (but not exclusively) semisynthesis as a tool for drug discovery, several industrial laboratories have published efforts to find next generation lincosamide antibiotics for clinical research9-11, but a lack of success of these efforts, and the diminishing profitability of antibiotics in general, have led to a marked diminution of industrial antibiotics discovery research.

In 2021, we reported a hybrid class of antibiotics comprising rigid bicyclic oxepanoprolinamide (OPP) southern residues12. Among OPP antibiotics was iboxamycin (IBX, Fig. 1a), which features substitution of position C4′13 of the bicycle with an iso-butyl side chain, the latter establishing Van der Waals (VDW) contacts within a conserved ribosomal cleft near the peptidyltransferase center (PTC)12. IBX and other OPP antibiotics have demonstrated promising activities against lincosamide-resistant bacterial strains. In 2024, we reported the discovery of the antibiotic cresomycin (CRM, Fig. 1a), which retains the bicyclic OPP residue of IBX, but also contains an extensively rigidified northern thiolincosamine residue, achieved by transannular fusion to form a unique 10-membered ring14. CRM exhibits striking efficacy against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial strains, including those expressing one or more of the known lincosamide resistance genes, or genes conferring resistance to other commonly used antibiotics. While we believe CRM represents a significant step toward addressing antimicrobial resistance (AMR), we considered and here report the results of a broader exploration of northern macrobicyclic variants sharing a common OPP southern scaffold. Our goal was to better define structure-activity relationships (SAR) within the northern macrobicyclic residue with a view toward three seemingly independent activity measures: (1) improved potency against antibiotic-resistant strains of Gram-positive bacteria, (2) improved potency against Gram-negative bacteria (relative to IBX and CRM; CLI is not active against Gram-negative bacteria), and (3) improved stability toward (murine) microsomal metabolism, as rapid sulfoxidation of the anomeric thioether groups of extant lincosamides leads to their rapid clearance in vivo15. As we describe below, we learned that it was possible to advance all three objectives in a single molecular series. This discovery was driven by the hypothesis that by introducing a substituent at position C11 of the macrocycle (see CRM, Fig 1a; this numbering differs from that of canonical lincosamides to properly represent the macrobicyclic scaffold) metabolism of the anomeric thioether might be attenuated as the result of steric occlusion and, potentially, stereoelectronic effects. Analysis of co-crystal structures of CRM bound to the bacterial ribosome suggested that an (11S)-substituent would project into the void of the nascent peptide exit tunnel and would therefore likely not impede target engagement. We selected the primary alcohol 1 (Fig. 1b) as our initial target for chemical synthesis because we imagined that it would serve as a versatile intermediate for chemical diversification by simple transformations that included, most consequentially, deoxyfluorination.

## Results

### Synthesis-enabled discovery of BT-33

To synthesize compound 1, we used the known α-thiogalactoside 216 (Fig. 1b, accessible on 100-g scale in five steps from D-galactose) as starting material. Michael addition of thiol 2 to an equimolar amount of the α,β-unsaturated aldehyde 317 proceeded smoothly in the presence of triethylamine. The aldehyde addition products, isolated together as a 1:1 mixture of diastereomers at position C11, were treated with methylenetriphenylphosphorane to afford alkenes 5, also a 1:1 diastereomeric mixture, inseparable by chromatography (56% combined yield, two steps). Selective deprotection of alkenes 5 at position C6 using an Otera organostannane catalyst18 was followed by oxidation of the resultant primary alcohols using the Dess-Martin periodinane reagent19. Condensation of the resultant aldehydes with Ellman’s (R)-t-butylsulfinamide20 afforded sulfinyl aldimines 6 (55% yield, three steps). Crotylation of the latter with crotylzinc chloride (4) at −109 °C favored the desired (7R)-epimer (d.r. 3:1) while setting the (6R)-stereochemistry with complete selectivity. Without purification, the diastereomeric mixture was subjected to ring-closing macrocyclization mediated by the Grubbs II catalyst21 to afford the targeted 10-membered bicyclic scaffold as the major product. After silyl deprotection, intermediate 1 was isolated by flash-column chromatography as a single diastereomer in 30% yield for the three-step sequence (150 mg prepared in a single batch).

With intermediate 1 in hand, we first investigated its deoxyfluorination, anticipating to obtain the primary fluoride 7 as product (Fig. 2a). However upon treatment of 1 with DAST22, we isolated instead the ring-expanded (11-membered ring) secondary alkyl fluoride 8 as the major product in 44% yield and, separately, the anticipated primary alkyl fluoride 7 in 34% yield, after benzoyl deprotection and preparative-HPLC purification. In retrospect, this result was not surprising, given that the electrophilic activation of the primary hydroxyl group within 1 could reasonably be anticipated to form an episulfonium intermediate, which then might be intercepted by fluoride at either the primary or secondary carbon atoms. Single crystal x-ray analysis of 8 unambiguously confirmed its structure and all stereochemical assignments. We next sought to assess the potential for 7 and 8 to furnish antibiotic candidates by coupling each respectively to the common OPP southern fragment 10 (Fig. 2b). This was accomplished by methanolysis of the sulfinamide function of each macrobicycle in the presence of HCl, then coupling the resultant ammonium salts with carboxylic acid 1023 using HATU and DIPEA24. N-Boc deprotection afforded separately the macrobicyclic OPP analogs BT-33 and (11S)-fluoromethyl cresomycin (11-FCH2-CRM).

### Structure-activity relationships within macrobicyclic OPPs

BT-33, an 11-membered macrobicyclic OPP antibiotic, potently inhibited the growth of multidrug-resistant bacteria when assessed against our standard screening panel of Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens (Fig. 3), with minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) typically one dilution lower (more potent) than CRM. To further explore structure-activity relationships, we synthesized 9-, 11-, and 12-membered macrobicyclic OPPs by straightforward adaptation of the synthetic route to BT-33 outlined in Figs. 1 and 2 above or, in the case of (11S)-BT-33, using a different, more scalable synthetic route25 (see supporting information for full experimental details). Macrocyclization reactions using the Grubbs II catalyst to form 11- and 12-membered macrocyclic products afforded separable mixtures of (E)- and (Z)-alkene isomers (favoring (E)-stereochemistry in both cases), while the macrocyclization reaction leading to the 9-membered analog (9Z) depicted in Fig. 3 formed exclusively the (Z)-alkene product. All products were purified by preparative-HPLC, the purified products were deprotected, and each northern fragment was separately coupled to the OPP residue 10. Salient points from analysis of the antimicrobial screening data and murine microsomal stability measurements follow.

The 11-membered β-fluoro sulfide BT-33 and the 10-membered β-fluoro sulfide 11-FCH2-CRM were found to be equipotent in our antimicrobial screening panel, and both had substantially enhanced half-lives when incubated with murine liver microsomes (Fig. 3, t1/2 = 100.9 min for BT-33 and t1/2 = 86.8 min for 11-FCH2-CRM) as compared to both CLI (t1/2 = 6.0 min) and CRM (t1/2 = 34.5 min). While the desfluoro analog of BT-33 (11Z) and BT-33 were found to be equipotent in Gram-positive bacterial strains, the activity of 11Z in two multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacterial strains was diminished relative to BT-33, as was its half-life in the presence of murine liver microsomes (t1/2 = 19.7 min). Inversion of the stereochemistry of the β-fluoride substituent ((11S)-BT-33) was found to reduce antimicrobial activity relative to BT-33 by as much as 4-fold. The BT-33 synthetic analog lacking the C7 methyl group (7-desMe-BT-33) was significantly less potent than BT-33 in antibacterial assays, especially in erm- and cfr-expressing strains of S. aureus (MIC increase of 16-fold), likely due to its diminished conformational rigidity relative to BT-33 (vide infra). Contraction of the macrocycle (9Z) or its expansion (12Z) diminished antimicrobial activity in both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial strains. 11-Membered macrobicyclic analogs of BT-33 with (E)-alkene stereochemistry (7R)-11E and (7S)-11E exhibited substantially reduced or no antibacterial activity, especially in clindamycin-resistant strains. Together, the data support the conclusions that the (11R)-fluorine atom of BT-33, its (7R)-methyl group, and the (Z)-geometry of the macrocyclic alkene are all essential features of this antibiotic.

### Broad-spectrum activity and pharmacokinetics of BT-33

To further profile the antibacterial activity of BT-33 relative to CLI and the previous OPP antibiotics CRM and IBX, we determined MIC values for all four compounds in parallel (Fig. 4a) using a broader panel of bacterial isolates, whose strains we selected on the basis of their strong resistance to CLI. The antibacterial activity of BT-33 was found to be superior to all comparands in both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial strains. Next, we evaluated BT-33 against antibiotics that target the PTC in a panel of linezolid-resistant staphylococcal clinical isolates that is made available from the Centers for Disease Control Antimicrobial Resistance Bank; BT-33 was found to inhibit the growth of 90% of isolates (MIC90) at a concentration of 1 μg·mL−1 (n = 30 isolates, Fig. 4b and Supplementary Table 2). The panel included isolates with cfr, erm, vgaA and/or lnuA lincosamide resistance determinants. We also evaluated BT-33 against approved antibiotics in a panel of multidrug-resistant enterococcal clinical isolates, where BT-33 exhibited an MIC90 of 0.25 μg·mL−1, a potency far exceeding any approved antibiotic comparand (n = 35 isolates, Fig. 4b, Supplementary Table 3). The panel included several strains of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium, an organism designated by the WHO as a high-priority pathogen for antibiotic development26. Next, we conducted single-dose pharmacokinetic studies of BT-33, CRM, and IBX in mice (Fig. 4c), where BT-33 exhibited an increased elimination half-life in plasma (6.80 h) as compared to CRM or IBX (4.66 and 2.05 h, respectively), reflecting in vitro liver microsomal stability measurements reported above.

### Structure of BT-33 bound to the bacterial ribosome

To determine the structure of BT-33 when bound to the bacterial ribosome, we co-crystallized BT-33 with purified Thermus thermophilus 70S ribosomes, synthetic mRNA, a non-hydrolyzable aminoacyl-tRNA analog (fMet-NH-tRNAiMet) for binding to the P-site, and deacylated tRNAPhe for binding to both the A- and E-sites. The electron density map (2F0-Fc) obtained from a crystal diffracting at 2.50-Å resolution unambiguously placed BT-33 in the PTC of the large ribosomal subunit in the canonical lincosamide binding pocket (Fig. 5a-c, Supplementary Table 4)27, and revealed a number of features common to ribosome-bound IBX and CRM12,14; namely, the C4′ iso-butyl side chain of the southern OPP residue of BT-33 was observed to make VDW contacts with nucleobases A2451 and G2452 (Fig. 5d), and the three hydroxyl groups of the northern macrobicyclic residue formed a hydrogen-bonding network with the nucleobases A2058, A2059, and the 2′-hydroxyl group of the nucleotide m2A2503 (Fig. 5e). As a unique feature, however, we observed that the fluorine atom and the bridging macrocycle makes a VDW contact with the π-face of the nucleobase G2505, an interaction that, we speculate, may well potentiate the antibacterial activity of BT-33 through enhanced target engagement. It was also interesting to note that ribosome-bound BT-33 adopts a conformation in which the S–C12 and C11–F bonds are antiperiplanar (Fig. 5f, the S–C12–C11–F dihedral angle is −177°), and that the macrobicyclic substructure rests in a conformation that is nearly identical to that observed in the single-crystal x-ray structure of intermediate 8 (see Fig. 2a above), supporting the idea that, like CRM, BT-33 is highly preorganized for ribosomal binding. These structures reveal that in the ribosome-bound 11-membered macrocyclic substructure of BT-33 the fluorine atom is optimally positioned for maximal electron withdrawal from the thioether bond (see the natural bond orbital analysis in Supplementary Table 1), while at the same time potentially enhancing engagement with the bacterial ribosome through a VDW contact.

### Conformational analyses of BT-33 and 7-desMe-BT-33 homologs

To better understand the conformational landscape of the 11-membered macrobicyclic antibiotics reported herein, we conducted variable-temperature 1H-NMR and vibrational circular dichroism (VCD) experiments and applied density-functional theory (DFT, B3PW91/6-31G(d)/PCM(methanol))28-31 to analyze the two acetamides 11 and 12, which served as simplified homologs of 7-desMe-BT-33 and BT-33, respectively. Both were trivially prepared by acetylation of the respective ammonium salts. Results from both theoretical and experimental studies were in striking accord. Shown in Fig. 6a are the results of DFT calculations, which revealed that the ground-state minimum-energy conformation of 12 (structure 12-C0) and its desmethyl derivative 11 (ground-state minimum structure 11-C0) were nearly superimposable. However, whereas conformation 12-C0 lies in an energetic well of ≥3.0 kcal·mol−1, the conformational landscape of 11 is populated by two additional conformers reflecting “alkene flipping” within the macrocycle at just +1.1 kcal/mol (structure 11-C1, Fig. 6a) and +2.3 kcal·mol−1 (structure 11-C2) higher energy than the ground-state conformer 11-C0. In the 1H-NMR spectrum of the desmethyl homolog 11 in CD3OD at 23 °C (Fig. 6b) the allylic proton signals were substantially broadened, suggesting conformational flexibility within the macrocycle. This was confirmed in variable-temperature 1H-NMR experiments, where at −70 °C in CD3OD the 1H-NMR spectrum of homolog 11 revealed two distinct conformers in ratio of 6.7:1, with observed chemical shifts in accordance with those predicted by DFT calculations32-34 for structures 11-C0 and 11-C1, respectively (Figs. 6b, Supplementary Figure 8). In sharp contrast, the 1H-NMR spectrum of homolog 12 at 23 °C revealed no such broadening of the allylic proton peaks (Fig. 6b), and its measured VCD spectrum in DMSO-d6 closely resembled the calculated VCD spectrum of the ground state conformer 12-C0 (MN15/cc-PVDZ/PCM(DMSO)35,36, Fig. 6c), providing evidence that the solution-state conformation of homolog 12 is that of the calculated ground state conformer 12-C037. Comparison of the macrobicyclic residues of ribosome-bound BT-33 (Fig. 5f) and the calculated ground-state conformation of homolog 12 (12-C0, Fig 6d) showed them to be essentially identical.

## Discussion

By using a versatile chemical synthesis platform for antibiotics discovery, we have learned that, like its bicyclic southern OPP scaffold, the northern macrobicyclic residue of BT-33 is exquisitely sensitive to chemical variation, as is evident from the structure-activity relationships reported herein. A salient single example is the molecule 7-desMe-BT-33, which exhibits substantially reduced antibacterial activity relative to BT-33, especially in multidrug-resistant bacterial strains (see Fig. 3, above). Although the C7-methyl group of BT-33 makes no observable contacts with the bacterial ribosome, as determined herein using x-ray crystallography, it does serve to lock the macrocyclic ring in a deep conformational well. While BT-33 and 7-desMe-BT-33 share essentially identical minimum-energy conformations, the existence of a low-lying (+1.1 kcal/mol) macrocyclic ring-flipped conformational variant in 7-desMe-BT-33 significantly reduces antibacterial activity. We believe the discovery that the 11-membered β-fluoro sulfide BT-33 exhibits improved potency relative to CRM against multidrug-resistant Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, as well as greatly improved metabolic stability, is significant. When reviewed, the pathway of chronological discovery from lincomycin to CLI, IBX, CRM, and now BT-33, makes evident the value of preorganization by structural rigidification as well as the importance of improved engagement with the molecular target, the bacterial ribosome, at least in this chemical series, if not more generally. Consistently, we have observed that as engagement with the ribosome has improved so, too, has activity against Gram-negative bacterial strains, which was not expected. The discovery process has been evolutionary and has benefited to an extent from serendipity. It is unlikely that a molecule such as BT-33, had it been conceived at the outset of our studies, would have been selected for chemical synthesis in light of its structural complexity. A series of chemical advances were necessary to enable the discovery of BT-33, reported herein. In a parallel submission, we describe further chemical advances that have enabled multi-gram scale synthesis of BT-33 in order to enable preclinical profiling studies25.

### Preparation of OPP analogs

Detailed protocols for the synthesis of macrobicyclic OPP analogs can be found in the Supplementary Information.

### Antimicrobial Susceptibility Assays

In vitro antibiotic susceptibility testing was performed using the broth microdilution method in accordance with the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines38. OPP analogs including BT-33 were synthesized as outlined in the supplementary information. IBX was synthesized as described in Mason et al23. CRM was synthesized as described in Wu et al14. Standard antibiotics used in this study were purchased from MilliporeSigma (Burlington, MA, USA). All test compounds and standard antibiotics were stored as dry powders at −20 °C prior to use. Working solutions of OPP analogs and comparator antibiotics were made at a concentration of 3.2 mg·mL−1 in DMSO immediately before use. Final antibiotic concentrations ranged from 32 – 0.06 μg·mL−1, in steps of two-fold dilutions, and maintained a final DMSO concentration of 2%.

Bacterial isolates were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC; Manassas, VA, USA), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention & Food and Drug Administration Antibiotic Resistance Isolate Bank (AR-Bank; Atlanta, GA, USA), JMI Laboratories Inc. (North Liberty, IA, USA), Micromyx repository (MMX; now Microbiologics, Kalamazoo, MI, USA), or Massachusetts Eye and Ear (Boston, MA, USA). All isolates were cryopreserved at −80 °C in glycerol stocks (20% glycerol in species-specific media). Unless otherwise noted, all isolates were revived from cryopreservation and sub-cultured on brain heart infusion agar (BD Diagnostics; Sparks, MD, USA) at 37 °C in 5 % CO2 for 24 hours prior to experimentation. Streptococcus spp. were sub-cultured on 5% blood agar plates and incubated at 37 °C in 5 % CO2.

For all organisms, 3–5 uniform colonies were picked from subcultures and suspended in 10 mL of cation-adjusted Mueller Hinton broth (ca-MHB, BD Diagnostics; Sparks, MD, USA) and incubated for 2–3 hours at 37 °C while being shaken at 250 rpm. The bacterial suspensions were then adjusted to a 0.5 MacFarland standard and further diluted 1:200 in ca-MHB to obtain a final test inoculum of 5 × 105 CFU mL−1. 96-well plates were seeded with DMSO solutions of OPP analogs and standard antibiotics in a two-fold serial dilution series. The final test inoculum of each organism in ca-MHB was then added and the plates were incubated for 18–24 hours at 37 °C. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing against Streptococcus spp. was performed using ca-MHB supplemented with 5% (v/v) defibrinated sheep blood. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing against P. aeruginosa was performed using iron-depleted ca-MHB according to CLSI guidelines as prescribed for cefiderocol.38 MIC values were represented as the modal value of biological triplicate experiments.

### Microsomal Stability

Hepatic microsomal stability was evaluated by incubating OPP analogs or CLI at a concentration of 1 μM with 1 mg/mL pooled mouse hepatic microsomes in potassium phosphate buffer (100 mM, pH 7.4). NADPH (final concentration of 1 mM) was added to initiate the reaction. Aliquots were removed at 0, 5, 10, 20, 40, and 60 minutes and added to acetonitrile (5 × v/v). The samples were filtered through a Millipore Multiscreen Solvinert 0.45 μm low binding PTFE hydrophilic filter plate by centrifugation and the concentration of remaining antibiotic was quantitated by LC-MS/MS at each time point. NADPH dependence of the reaction was evaluated with −NADPH samples. Data was log-transformed and represented as half-lives.

### Single Dose Pharmacokinetics in Mice

Single dose pharmacokinetic studies were approved by Pharmaron Beijing’s Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) and conducted in accordance with Pharmaron Beijing’s IACUC guidelines (Protocol approval number PK-M-07182024) at Pharmaron, Ningbo, CN (OLAW assurance number: F23-00575) following standard protocols. Female CD-1 mice (4-6 weeks, Vital River Laboratories, CN) were housed with a 12-hour light/dark cycle, 20–26 °C ambient temperature and 40-70% humidity during this study. ### X-ray Crystal Structure of 8

Data was collected from a crystal mounted on a diffractometer at 100 K. The intensities of the reflections were collected by means of a Bruker D8 Venture diffractometer (MoKα radiation, λ=0.71073 Å), and equipped with an Oxford Cryosystems nitrogen flow apparatus. The collection method involved 0.5° scans in ω at 11° in 2θ. Data integration down to 0.77 Å resolution was carried out using SAINT V8.40A (Bruker AXS APEX3, Madison, Wisconsin, 2019) with reflection spot size optimization. Absorption corrections were made with the program SADABS40. The structure was solved by the Intrinsic Phasing methods and refined by least-squares methods again F2 using SHELXT-201941 with OLEX 2 interface42. Non-hydrogen atoms were refined anisotropically, and hydrogen atoms were allowed to ride on the respective atoms. Crystal data as well as details of data collection and refinement, geometric parameters, and hydrogen-bond parameters are listed in section 3. The Ortep plots were produced with SHELXL-2018 program, and the three-dimensional supramolecular architecture drawing was produced with Accelrys DS Visualizer 2.06.

### X-ray Crystal Structure of BT-33 in Complex with T. thermophilus 70S Ribosome

Wild-type 70S ribosomes from T. thermophilus (strain HB8) were prepared as described previously43-45. Synthetic mRNA with the sequence 5’-GGC-AAG-GAG-GUA-AAA-AUG-UUC-UAA-3' containing Shine-Dalgarno sequence followed by the P-site methionine (AUG) and A-site phenylalanine (UUC) codons was obtained from Integrated DNA Technologies (Coralville, IA, USA). Ribosome complexes with mRNA and tRNAs were formed by incubating 5 μM T. thermophilus 70S ribosomes with 10 μM mRNA at 55°C for 10 minutes, followed by the addition of 20 μM fMet-tRNAiMet and 20 μM deacylated tRNAPhe substrates12,14,44. For the ribosome complexes containing BT-33, the antibiotic was added to a final concentration of (125 μM), and the complex was left at room temperature for an additional 15 minutes prior to crystallization. Ribosome complexes were prepared in the buffer containing 5 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 7.6), 50 mM KCl, 10 mM NH4Cl, and 10 mM Mg(OAc)2, and then crystallized in the buffer containing 100 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.6), 2.9% (w/v) PEG-20K, 9-10% (v/v) MPD, 175 mM arginine, 0.5 mM β-mercaptoethanol. Crystals were grown by the vapor diffusion method in sitting drops at 19 °C, then stabilized and cryo-protected stepwise using a series of buffers with increasing MPD concentrations (25%, 30%, 35%) until reaching the final concentration of 40% (v/v) MPD as described previously12,14,44. The final 40% MPD stabilization buffer contained 125 μM BT-33. After stabilization, crystals were flash-frozen using a nitrogen cryo-stream at 80 K (Oxford Cryosystems, UK).

Collection and processing of the X-ray diffraction data, model building, and structure refinement were performed as previously described12,14,44. Diffraction data were collected at beamlines 24ID-C and 24ID-E at the Advanced Photon Source (Argonne National Laboratory). A complete dataset was collected using 0.979Å X-ray irradiation at 100K from multiple regions of the same crystal, using 0.3-degree oscillations. Raw data were integrated and scaled using the XDS software package (version from Jan 10, 2022) 46. Molecular replacement was performed using PHASER from the CCP4 program suite (version 7.0) 47. The search model was generated from the previously published structures of the T. thermophilus 70S ribosome with bound mRNA and aminoacylated tRNAs (PDB entry 6XHW) 48. Initial molecular replacement solutions were refined by rigid-body refinement with the ribosome split into multiple domains, followed by positional and individual B-factor refinement using the PHENIX software (version 1.17) 49. Non-crystallographic symmetry restraints were applied to four parts of the 30S ribosomal subunit (head, body, spur, and helix 44) and four parts of the 50S subunit (body, L1-stalk, L10-stalk, and C-terminus of the L9 protein). Initial PDB model and CIF restraints for BT-33 were generated using PHENIX eLBOW (v1.17) 49. The final PDB model was built in Coot (version 0.8.2)50. The statistics of data collection and refinement are compiled in Supplementary Table 4. All figures showing atomic models were rendered using PyMOL Molecular Graphics System software (version 1.8.6, Schrödinger, www.pymol.org).

### Computational Conformational Analysis

Conformer generation was performed using the Monte Carlo plus Minimization (MCMM) method in Macromodel 9.951,52 with the OPLS 2005 force field.53 An initial cutoff of +25 kcal/mol was used to prune candidate structures. For each compound, generated conformations were subjected to DFT geometry optimization and duplicates were removed. All DFT calculations were performed with Gaussian 16, Revision A.0354. Geometry optimization of all structures was carried out using the B3PW91 functional with a basis set of 6-31G(d)28 on all atoms, incorporating the PCM solvation model29-31 with methanol as the solvent. Frequency calculations were performed to confirm the nature of the stationary points and to evaluate zero-point vibration energy (ZPVE) and thermal corrections at 298 K. To assess the effect of solvent, structures were reoptimized with water, chloroform, or DMSO implicit solvation, and the relative energies and ordering of conformers were found to be similar to those from the chloroform calculations (Supplementary Fig. 7).

Computed structures were illustrated using GaussView 655 or CYLView 20.56 Isotropic chemical shieldings were calculated using the gauge-invariant atomic orbital (GIAO)32-34,57 approach with methanol as the solvent and using empirical linear scaling for comparison with experimental shifts. Vibrational circular dichroism and infrared spectra (energies and intensities) were calculated35 using the MN15 functional and the cc-PVDZ basis set on all atoms36, using molecular geometries re-optimized at this level of theory and incorporating the PCM solvation model with DMSO as the solvent.

**Authors:** Elena V. Aleksandrova; Kelvin J. Y. Wu; Ben I. C. Tresco; Egor A. Syroegin; Erin E. Killeavy; Samson M. Balasanyants; Maxim S. Svetlov; Steven T. Gregory; Gemma C. Atkinson; Andrew G. Myers; Yury S. Polikanov
